newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria, buoyed by oil prices, cuts budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: Algeria, buoyed by oil prices, cuts budget deficit.

text.p: Algeria, helped by soaring crude oil prices and a buoyant dollar, forecast a pruned budget deficit of 64.72 billion dinars ($1.15 billion) in 1997 from an original 84.70 billion dinars ($1.51 billion).

The government in a mini-budget, to be debated this week by the National Assembly (lower house), said total revenue would increase to 881.5 billion dinars ($15.74 billion) against 946.22 billion dinars ($16.89 billion) expenditure.

The government figures, reported on Tuesday by the official Algerian news agency APS, showed initial forecasts had put revenue and expenditure respectively at 829.4 billion dinars ($14.8 billion) and 914.1 billion dinars ($16.32 billion).
"This readjustment of the budget is due to a change of the economic and financial parameters, namely those with significant weight," said APS.

The official data showed that the volume and value of the country's oil and gas exports increased respectively by 7.9 percent and 13.1 percent in the first five months of 1997 compared to the same period in 1996.
The government said it expects oil and gas exports to yield $12.5 billion in 1997, up by $1.0 billion on its initial forecasts.
The value of Algeria's oil and gas exports in 1996 were $12.6 billion, up 29 percent from the previous year, thanks mainly to increased crude oil prices.
Then Algeria earned an average $21.5 per barrel against a budgeted average of $16-17 per barrel.
The cabinet said the government had based the initial budget for 1997 on a conservative oil price of $17.50 a barrel.
Algeria, an Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) member, has a quota of 750,000 barrels per day. The country also exports about 30 billion cubic metres of gas a year.
The cabinet this week unveiled a three-year programme setting the value of Algeria's gas and oil exports at $15 billion a year in addition to $2.0 billion from non-hydrocarbon exports.
The government listed other political and economic factors as having mixed effects on the budget.
The soaring dollar and de-stocking by increasingly confident local firms had helped lower imports in the first five months. But the government lost on the value added tax levied on imported goods.
VAT on imported products and other excise taxes were expected to slump by 18.8 billion dinars ($335 million) to 124.7 billion dinars ($2.22 billion) for the whole year, APS said.
Government coffers are expected to swell by an additional 56 billion dinars ($1.0 billion) to 507 billion dinars from the exported oil and gas taxes, official figures showed.

Government employees' salary rises, subsidies for the country's retirement fund, underwriting credits to state-owned firms, the costs of next October's planned local elections and refurbishment of the parliament ripped holes in the budget.
The spending on the extra items amounts to nearly 29 billion dinars ($500 million), official data showed.
Algeria's budget for 1996 set total expenditure of at 848.6 billion dinars and revenue at 749.2 billion.
